Recent national studies published by federal government agencies, national laboratories, and research organizations demonstrate that significant transmission expansion is the lowest-cost option to meet growing demand and maintain grid reliability (U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) 2024; Larson et al. 2021; Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) 2021; Denholm et al. 2022; U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) 2023). Despite these findings, transmission capacity additions across the United States have declined steadily over the last 10 years. Focused primarily on incremental reliability needs, only 3,300 circuit-miles of new or upgraded transmission and 70 circuit-miles of interregional transmission were added annually, on average, from 2011 to 2020 (U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) 2023). By comparison, studies such as the U.S. Department of Energy’s National Transmission Planning Study estimate annual additions of more than 4,000 circuit-miles of new high-voltage transmission can unlock the lowest-cost mix of transmission, generation, and storage resources to meet growing system needs through 2035 (U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) 2024). The slowing of additions of transmission has led to increasing congestion across the grid and a backlog of interconnection requests. The result has been nearly 12,000 projects and over 2,500 gigawatts waiting in interconnection queues by the end of 2023, rising interconnection costs, longer generation project development timelines, and an increasing number of project cancellations (Rand et al. 2024). The challenges with developing bulk transmission can be broadly characterized by the “three Ps” —planning, permitting, and paying (cost allocation) (Gavan and Gramlich 2021). Planning is a challenge because transmission exhibits large economies of scale and identifying least-cost transmission investments requires long-term, multivalue planning and coordination across multiple jurisdictions and wide geographic areas. Permitting a bulk transmission project is a multiyear process that typically requires numerous authorizations and compliance with a complex set of U.S. federal, state, and local requirements (U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) 2023). Paying, or cost allocation, for transmission—the focus of this report—is often cited as the hardest of the “three Ps” (Gavan and Gramlich 2021). Assigning the costs of transmission projects to network users is highly contentious because these costs can have a direct impact on energy prices and ratepayer bills.
